messages.author: d0591fb2a98d1e44
messages.subject: Unit trace matrix
parts:
Can I use the transform parameters section of code to make it so that the trace of a matrix is one? If I have:

parameters{
  matrix[numRows,numCols] X;
}
transformed parameters{
   matrix[numRows,numCols] X_unitTrace;
   real traceX;

   traceX<-trace(X);
   X_unitTrace<-multiply(1/traceX,X)
}

If I have a prior for X in my model section, but then work with X_unitTrace, will I be using a matrix that has a trace of one?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts: That is valid syntax but you have to make sure that the prior on X breaks the scale indeterminacy.

messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts: I'm not familiar with scale indeterminacy. Is there a standard way to go about doing that?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts:
On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 1:09:20 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
I'm not familiar with scale indeterminacy. Is there a standard way to go about doing that?

If you were to multiply X by some a > 0, then X_unitTrace is unaffected. Thus, the likelihood has no information to distinguish between X and aX. So the prior has to distinguish between X and aX in order for the posterior to be proper. For example, independent normal priors with known standard deviation would do the trick but not if the standard deviation were unknown and had an improper uniform prior. A proper prior on the standard deviation would work, but you might not get very good sampling if it is weak.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Unit trace matrix
parts:
Firstly when you divided by the trace of X you need to
take into account the Jacobian (d/dtheta 1 / Tr(X(theta)) )
— you should see a warning about this.

Scale indeterminacy is just as Ben said — many parameter
settings will give the same likelihood, so the posterior will
be non identified (it will stretch to infinity) causing poor fits.

In any case you might as well use the rank-2 tensor decomposition —

X = (Tr(X) / n) * I + S + A

where S and A are symmetric and antisymmetric matrices, respectively.

You’ll have to declare n(n-1)/2 parameters for the symmetric and
asymmetric parts and then build up the matrix in transformed parameters,
but you’ll be guaranteed to have a unit-trace matrix without any
worried about scale indeterminacy.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts:
On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 2:52:15 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
I'm sorry. I'm not entirely sure what "scale indeterminacy" means.

It is just how I defined it in my last post: X and a * X imply the same likelihood. So, the data alone cannot distinguish proposals for X from proposals for a * X and in the absence of a proper prior on X, you would have an improper posterior distribution.
Do I need to priors for both X and X_unit trace?
No.

parameters{
  matrix[dimensions] X;
}
transformed parameters{
   cov_matrix[dimensions] X_unitTrace;
   real traceX;

   traceX<-trace(X);
   X_unitTrace<-multiply(1/traceX,X);
}
model{
X~wishart(nu,Sigma2); #nu and Sigma2 are constants and Sigma2 is the Identity matrix

#The rest of the code uses X_unitTrace rather than X
}

This would be acceptable --- if X were declared as a cov_matrix[dimensions] --- because the degrees of freedom and dispersion matrix are constants. Thus, the Wishart PDF would evaluate to different numbers for X and a * X for any a != 1.

However, these trace-constrained Wisharts have been known to lead to poor sampling and in my opinion, do not make much sense for a probability model. I prefer to declare a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix (L) and a simplex (pi) to represent the variances (which necessarily sum to 1).

data {
  int<lower=1> dimensions;
  real<lower=0> eta;
  vector<lower=0>[dimensions] alpha;
}
parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[dimensions] L;
  simplex[dimensions] pi;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[dimensions,dimensions] X_unitTrace;
  {
    vector[dimensions] sds;
    for (i in 1:dimensions) sds[i] <- sqrt(pi[i]);
    X_unitTrace <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(
                   diag_pre_multiply(sds, L) ); 
  }
}
model {
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(eta);
  pi ~ dirichlet(alpha);
  // now do the likelihood of the data as a function of X_unitTrace
}

Ben

On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 1:09:20 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
I'm not familiar with scale indeterminacy. Is there a standard way to go about doing that?

If you were to multiply X by some a > 0, then X_unitTrace is unaffected. Thus, the likelihood has no information to distinguish between X and aX. So the prior has to distinguish between X and aX in order for the posterior to be proper. For example, independent normal priors with known standard deviation would do the trick but not if the standard deviation were unknown and had an improper uniform prior. A proper prior on the standard deviation would work, but you might not get very good sampling if it is weak.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts:
On Thursday, July 2, 2015 at 4:19:22 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
Do you have any sources that you can recommend I learn about this in more detail? I guess I know enough about Bayesian statistics to be dangerous. I chose Wisharts mostly because it returned a matrix I was looking for (ie. symmetric positive definite).

A lot of people are that way. It is true that the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions are for random variables that are symmetric and positive definite. However, that fact alone is insufficient to justify their use because for any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma there are an infinite number of matrix decompositions where Sigma = Z * Z'. So literally any prior distribution on the elements of Z implies a prior distribution over the symmetric and positive definite matrix Sigma.

If so, why are the Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions essentially the only distributions for symmetric and positive definite matrices that you read about in the Bayesian literature? The sole reason is that they are conjugate with a multivariate normal distribution, so Gibbs samplers can do updates of the symmetric and positive definite matrix by drawing from a Wishart or inverse Wishart full-conditional distribution. That raises the fundamental point that Stan does not do Gibbs sampling because Gibbs sampling can easily be antithetical to the goal of getting an adequate number of effective samples from a posterior distribution. Also, 25 years of Gibbs sampling has conditioned people into asking "What prior distribution is conjugate?" instead of "What prior distribution reflects my beliefs about a parameter?"

So, what are your beliefs about this symmetric positive definite matrix? If you are like 99% of people, you don't really have any. Presuming so, what would be an uninformative prior for a symmetric positive definite matrix? We can't really answer that question for an arbitrary symmetric positive definite matrix, but we can answer it for a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix. (What we at Stan call) The LKJ distribution with shape parameter eta = 1 is jointly uniform among among all correlation matrices of dimension K. You could read the paper 2009 by Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe referenced in the Stan manual but it is as frustrating as it is fundamental to multivariate probability. The main implication is that it allows you to put a uniform prior on a symmetric positive definite correlation matrix.

A correlation matrix has a trace of K, whereas you need a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1 for some reason. That is no problem because any symmetric positive definite matrix Sigma can be decomposed as Sigma = Delta * Lambda * Delta where Delta is a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and Lambda is a correlation matrix. The i-th diagonal element of Sigma is the i-th variance, namely Delta[i,i]^2, and you need the variances to sum to 1. A simplex is a random vector that is constrained to be positive and sums to 1, which is perfect for your situation. So, what are your prior beliefs about this simplex? If you are like 90% of people, you don't really have any, in which case a Dirichlet prior distribution with all concentration parameters (contained in the fixed vector alpha) equal to 1 reflects your prior belief that all simplexes are equally probable a priori, i.e. it is a uniform distribution over a simplex. The other 10% set all the elements of alpha equal to some other positive constant besides 1 to reflect non-uniform but symmetric beliefs about the simplex.

In summary, it is quite possible to utilize a uniform prior distribution over a correlation matrix and a uniform prior distribution over a simplex, and multiply some stuff together to obtain a symmetric positive definite matrix with a trace of 1. To do that, in my previous post, I set sds[i] = sqrt(pi[i]) where pi is a simplex and implicitly set Lambda = L * L' where L is a Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix Lambda. Then the line
X_unitTrace <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose( diag_pre_multiply(sds, L) );

efficiently does what in R code would be

diag(sqrt(pi)) %*% L %*% t(L) %*% diag(sqrt(pi))

The remaining wrinkle is that we want a uniform distribution on the correlation matrix Lambda, but Lambda is not actually a parameter of the model. Rather its Cholesky factor, L, is. By applying a multivariate change-of-variables, it is possible to work out what the prior distribution of L is if you have an LKJ prior on Lambda = L * L' . We call this log-prior the lkj_corr_cholesky distribution, but it needs to be called explicitly in the model block (presumably with eta = 1).

It so happens that --- under these priors --- simplexes and Cholesky factors of correlation matrices tend to be pretty easy for Stan to efficiently draw samples of, although, to repeat my fundamental point, not via Gibbs sampling. That is really just icing on the cake but in part follows from the process of thinking carefully about what probability distributions reflect your (lack of) beliefs and people like us thinking carefully about what multivariate transformations do to the geometry of the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from. It also happens to be the case that Wishart and inverse Wishart distributions often do unspeakable acts to the (unconstrained) parameter space that Stan is sampling from, so there is not only essentially no reason to use them in Stan (because Stan does not do Gibbs sampling) but also a strong reason to not use them in Stan (because Stan often can't sample them very effectively).

Ben

Just a slight correction:  Yes, Wisharts are in the literature for mathematical convenience, but the use of the Wishart distribution, at least in theoretical statistics, predates the Gibbs sampler.  Even before the Gibbs sampler, conjugacy was considered to be a good thing:  not because it simplified the Gibbs sampler but because it simplified analytic calculations.

P.S. to Ben:  OK if I blog your speech here?

The sole reason is that they are conjugate with a multivariate normal distribution, so Gibbs samplers can do updates of the symmetric and positive definite matrix by drawing from a Wishart or inverse Wishart full-conditional distribution.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts:
On Saturday, August 1, 2015 at 5:51:01 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
I am confident that my initial value for my parameter, which is a positive semidefinite matrix, is close to the actual parameter. Will changing the value of eta, which I currently have set to 1, in the lkj_corr_cholesky(eta) distribution constrain closer to the initial value? If so, would increasing or decreasing be better?

Only if your initial value is the identity matrix. The LKJ density does not have a location parameter, but its mode is the identity matrix for any eta > 1 and is more peaked for larger values of eta.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Unit trace matrix
parts:
On Saturday, August 1, 2015 at 6:18:23 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
Given that I know my initial point is a good guess, is the lkj_corr_cholesky distribution a good choice?

Compared to what? We don't know (the properties) of any other distribution for correlation matrices? Technically, you could apply the LKJ transformation and its Jacobian to any distribution for the partial correlations to get another density for a correlation matrix, but the only one that has been analyzed is the symmetric beta prior proposed in the LKJ paper.

Ben

I think the problem here is that you haven’t defined your criteria for “reasonably good”.
In particular, it’s not clear if that criteria is consistent with your posterior distribution
(i.e. if your posterior concentrates around that value).
